segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: OK, we are gonna talk for little. I'm gonna ask you some questions. I'm gonna follow what they have written down. The first question I'm gonna ask you is what is your name in English?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Jimmy Duncan.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What is your name in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: My mom and dad just call me Jim, just a shorter version, or Jimmy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where were you born, and what year were you born?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I was born in Tahlequah, but then I grew up in Dahlonegah. I'm 68 years old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you grew up around that area. Now, what was the name of the place you grew up at?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I don’t really understand what you said... Oh! I grew up in Dahlonegah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you grew up in a big area. All I know is they call it (Getiyo).

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now where you grew up, like you say (Getiyo), you didn't go anywhere else?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, sometimes I stayed at my dad’s where I grew up. It was a little room, and whatever happened, I had a hard life growing up. My grandma and her sister pretty much raised me when I was growing up. (Kandi) was her name, that's who I was living with.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, that’s who pretty much raised you.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah. When my dad was a heavy drinker, we always got into it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yes, we have all been through that kind of life.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, when I was 12, 13, 14 years old, he told me I need to leave, but I was still going to school. But that's when I left. My mom was still around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, the beer can really mess things up.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yes, me myself, I used to drink. When I was about 50 years old, I quit drinkin'; it's been almost 20 years since I quit drinkin'.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was the reason you became an alcoholic? When you started working, was it what was going on in your life, or was it because you thought, “My dad was an alcoholic, so I'm gonna be same way”?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, I didn't think like that, because I was working at the time. I had been working for 26 years at Greenleaf, they call it. That's where I quit working when I was 60 years old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What did you do when you were working at Greenleaf?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I was just working in production, where they start at propagation. That's where I was working. They start everyone there. That's pretty much ‘bout all I did there. I worked very hard when I was growing up, hauling hay, and I was making good money and nowadays, I guess people just quit doing it because all you see is big round bales these days. Back in the day, you could make good money doin' that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was hard work early morning and all day.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yes, if it was dry, then it was 10 or 11 or til it got dark before we got done. We hauled a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When I first started, they put up at the very top where I was a stacker. Boy, there were wasp nests right there. I thought, “That's why they put me there!” [laughs] But it was really hot, too.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I just put them up there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you have any children?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Four boys and one girl.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Are they all grown up?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, they are all grown up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, they are all grown up now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So now, they are feeding you now. [laughs]

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: [laughs] Mom and Dad are all they know, these kids these days. They really don't want to work, but one works at Baldor, which is good, and he is making really good money. And then one of my daughters, she said, “Dad,” - when she was going to school, she had a baby boy, but she was still living at the house and still going to school. And she ended up finishing school, and that's when she said, “Dad, I'm finished school now. I'm gonna get out and go find me a job.” I told her OK, and from then on, she has grown up. After she finished school, she moved out, and she lives in Stilwell. She has three boys. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yes.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I bet it cost you a lot of money at Christmas.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, they really don't like that, but that one boy, Tyler is his name, but myself I call him Littleman, he's the oldest one. When they basketball, with that loud sound he said his ears hurt. That's why I feel sorry for him and take him places, but myself I really like watching basketball.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We have three granddaughters. The oldest one is 22 years old, but when she was little, I was teaching her how to work. If I needed them to help me with something, I tell her to come help me. When we got done, I ask her, “Well, how much did it cost?” “Forty dollars!” [laughs] That's all she knew [laughs]. Even if she helped me a little bit, forty dollars.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I told my kids to come help me when they come to the house. I tell them we gotta work, and their momma asks them, “He makes you work?” “Yeah, Grandpa does, but he pays us.” [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout your relatives? Are they still alive?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, there two of us boys and one girl, but my brother he don't hardly come around. He's about 60, 64 years old. He barely gets around anymore. He has to use a walker to get around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Does he have arthritis or something?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I think so, but then again, he's a really big guy, and he has heart problems. His name is Joe. Even though I'm the oldest, they didn't give me that, and my sister, she’s ‘bout 60. She is not in very good condition either, and I think she’s getting crippled also. She’s a little better - she found out that she was gonna have to do things herself. But she has a home caretaker that watches out for her. And they ask me, because I speak Cherokee. My grandma, my father, they all speak to me in Cherokee, but when I started in school and working, it seemed like it was more English. That's when I started losing some Cherokee. I was tellin' my wife, like these Mexicans, when they work somewhere, that's all they know. But then, the Cherokee, they didn't want to work. I started to realize I started losing my language because I wasn't using it, and my wife, she didn't speak that much Cherokee. She can understand it but she can't speak it very well. Every once in a while, I run into someone and speak Cherokee. I still try to speak Cherokee, but sometimes I forget, and then it comes back to me. If I think about it, when someone talks to me in Cherokee and I'm a little slow sometimes, I guess it's because I'm getting old. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Every one of us are just getting old [laughs]… what was your parents’ name?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: My father’s name was Joe, my mother’s name is (Ahoge), and my grandma’s name was (Alle). My grandfather’s name was (Qwock). My other grandmother, I really never knew her. My mother worked at Cherokee Nation in Stilwell when they first opened, and that's where she retired to. I think she worked there 40 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She worked there very long time at Cherokee Nation.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: You know when they used to give you points? She never was late, not even two minutes or five minutes. And my father, he was a police officer in Stilwell, but he wasn't a very big officer. He was just a helper. He worked for ‘bout 20 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He worked for them that long?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: His heart finally gave up on him.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did your parents grow up at, in what area?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: My father grew up around Salem. He grew up around the Cochran family, that's where he grew up, around that family, and my mother, she grew up around that area as well.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, Salem is where they grew up.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, Salem.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What clan did your parents come from, ahoe or longhair or ahniewod or the bird clan the seven clan Cherokees? Or maybe they never told you what clan you're from?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, they never told me what clan I was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it's surprising that they never told you what clan you were.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I don't remember them tellin' me what clan I was from. Maybe I'll find out later on [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout your grandmother we was talkin' ‘bout earlier, where did she grow up? Did she grow up around Salem, too?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Just down that road from Salem is ‘bout where she grew up, she got into it with her sister a long time ago. When they got into it, they were living really close. What was the name? Gah-lee, I can't remember! She never really went to town unless she went for meat or groceries. When her and her sister got into it, she went to Stilwell and that's where she lived. Whenever she lived in Dahlonegah, I lived with her then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout your parents? Where did they first meet? Do you know where?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: [laughs] I guess around Stilwell. My father told me, “I thought I was gonna go visit just for a little bit, but they left me over there.” So he just went to school there till eighth grade. He thought he was there just for a little bit, but they just left him over there, and that's where he grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, that's where they met each other.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: They always used to go to Colorado. They used to have pictures of him when he used to be a boxer. I always got to Golden Glove, but he never won. He always got beat up. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, me too. I was in Joplin, they were taking me to Golden Glove, but something happened. I couldn't go, but then they took the white boy instead. Right at the start of the fight, he got knocked out. He got beat up by a black guy. [laughs] If I had gone, that black guy would've dragged me around everywhere. [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: He said a black guy always beat him up. He said the black guy was really big and always beat him up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This one Cherokee boy, he was a heavyweight. He won the Golden Glove. He won the whole thing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout your last name? What was your last name?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Duncan…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You don't know where the last name came from?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, there are a bunch of them around Bell area. We are all related, but myself, I grew up around this area, not Bell. But when I tell them my last name, they always say I'm from Bell. I tell them “No, that's not where I grew up, but every one of them I'm related to, and my father, that's where he's from.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I know one guy, his name is (Leo Duncan). Do you know him?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I know him. We are related, but I hadn't seen him in a long time. But yeah, when we were younger, we didn't get along. The ones that grew around Bell and the ones that grew up around here, when we were all growing up, we always used to fight. [laughs]. John and the ones that live around Dahlonegah, sometimes we used to fight, then everyone gonna fight. [laughs]. One day, I seen him, that one boy, so I asked him, if I ever seen him somewhere we were always gonna fight. As soon as he seen me, he was always ready to fight. One day, I seen he was already coming my way. I told him, “Boy, John,” I said. He said, “No, we are gonna fight.” I said, “I told you, you can't ever whup me.” I told him that he's never whupped me before. [laughs]. “And you're not gonna whup me now, either,” I told him. [laughs]. But I told him, “I'm gonna ask you one question: how come you always want to fight me?” I asked him, and he looked at me. He said, “I don't know.” And I told him, “Boy, myself either!” [laughs] That's when we shook hands, and that was the last time we got into a fight. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So y'all became friends then. [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, he didn't know what we was fighting for, and I didn't either! [laughs]. You know, there is a dog that's always mad at you, and it's always gonna chase you around everywhere, if you do something to it all the time. And every time the dog sees you, it's gonna chase you, ain't it? [laughs]. That's how he was like. He didn't know what we was fighting for. If we’d seen each other at the bar or just anywhere, he was always wanting to fight me, and he never did whup me. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: [laughs] Y'all became friends then. [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, we became good friends, and we were first cousins. [laughs]. All the time, that boy, he always wanted to fight me. [laughs]. Just because I didn't grow up in Bell, that's why they didn't like me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you whupped him for no reason all the time. [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: My wife always said, “Well, did you fight again?” She asked in English [laughs] I tell her yeah, I got into a fight with John again. [laughs]. “Well, did you whup him again?” she asked. I told her, “Yeah, I whupped him again.” [laughs]. Sometimes we would greet each other if I’d seen him from a distance, but then if he’d seen me somewhere, then he wanted to fight. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He wanted to fight you. [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: He would be asometimes. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout like they call me Guy, how ‘bout you when you were growing up? They didn't call you by a different name?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, they just call me Jim.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They didn't ever call you Chooch?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, no, they didn't ever call me that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes, they give you a name like Chooch, or sometimes as you're growing up, they give you names.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Sometimes if you're mean, you never know what they are gonna name you. [laughs]. They always say, “Well, Jimmy done it again. He got into something again,” they always used to say. Even when I was younger, that's what they would say. I never knew what my name was. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, sometimes they called me crazy. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout when you were growing up? Your grandparents didn't ever tell you any awesome stories? Or your parents, they didn't ever tell you any good stories? Like if they seen things or just anything?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Long time ago, they never really told me anything when I was growing up, and what all they went through growing up. Me, when I was growing up long time ago, we really never had anything. There was one white man who had a store. He always helped us out. If it wasn't for him, we probably wouldn't have ever made it through.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So that white guy always helped y'all out?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: And for our house, we just lived right by there. There wasn't that many of us there, but food-wise, our father when he worked, he would buy us some food. We really didn't have much. We grew up living a hard life. But when we were kids, all we did was have fun, and we really never fought again. ‘Bout the only thing, if we had grease and flour, you would never go hungry…

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes my mother, if we didn't have anything but flour, she would make us bread. They would get really big, and if we had salt, we would put it on our bread and we would eat it.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, me too. Sometimes I do that, put salt on it, and sometimes I put onion on it like a sandwich. And if that’s warm, it's really good to eat.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, my wife, whenever we are home, that's what she makes for us. And that's what we eat, and then she makes water gravy, too.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: That's pretty much what we eat, too, and hog meat and sometimes pig feet and fried potatoes, and then sometimes boiled potatoes. I would make a sandwich out of it, and my wife never really knew how to do that, but then she learned how to. Also, I make bean patties sometimes when they get cold, and I put salt on them. It's pretty much the same if you mix it with bread.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what my wife did if we had beans left over. Boy, we just put salt on them. Boy, they were good. Boy, these days kids don't know nothing about that.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, my little boy, well, I don't know if you can call him little anymore, if I'm having some beans and potatoes, boy, he will eat a lot. And his boys, when they eat, they will say, “Um, this is food!” [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That's good food, and when we were kids, me and my sister, I didn't know that our life was hard. We always were laughing and feeling good, even if we just got water gravy, we were OK with that. I guess our mom and dad knew how hard it was growing up.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I myself, when you got clothes, like my jeans would have holes in them and my shoes would be worn out, and you know when I went to school, I see the other kids wearing nice clothes, and that's when I knew that us Cherokees had it pretty hard. Then I would ask Mom and Dad how come we didn't have nice clothes, and they would tell me that things were hard for us. Then I would see that it was hard for us. That's what I would tell everyone.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah sometimes I would get a new pair of pants once a month, and after I got home from school, I would have to change into my old pair of jeans, because I would be saving my new pair of jeans, and my shoes also. [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: That's the same way we did when we went to church.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And that was the same way with socks, too. My socks would have holes in them. [laughs]

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, me too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nowadays you go to Walmart, you will see pants with holes in them for sale.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, they sell clothes like that and pay bout 40/60 dollars for those kinds of clothes. [laughs] I told my wife I wouldn't pay that much for clothes that have holes in them. [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Boy, if we had some, we would be selling them, ain't it? [laughs]

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: My two boys, I lost one of them when he was 50 years old. My oldest, that hit me pretty hard. This lady of mine is my second wife. My first wife, we never got married, but this second one, we got married. And when we got separated, my boys were not very big, but my oldest one said that he was going with Dad, and the other went the other way. But I was working at the time, and I told myself that as long as I'm working, they will have the things they need. I always bought them nice clothes and things they needed, but my little one, he said he was going with his momma, so I told him OK, but I told him, “Just remember, this will always be your home, always.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Doors will always be open, you told him.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I told my youngest son before he went with his momma, I told him, “You know when you go that way, you ain't gonna be wearing clothes like that.” And it wasn't even two years, he came back and said, “Dad, can I come back?” I told him, “Yes, I told you this is always your home.” And then I was raising two kids again. I used to cook real good for them. They didn't care - they were playing everywhere, then I'd be home by myself, eating all by myself. [laughs]. “Boy, I work hard, then I come home and cook for you boys, and you boys don't even eat!” [laughs]. “Well,” they said, “we want to play.” They always told me. [laughs] I said oh, OK. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout the stories that come from old Cherokee? Your granny ever told you what happened to her parents back in the old days?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, not really, she never really told me anything. I barely remember, but I can't really say or remember.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout where you grew up when you were a boy? What did the area or place look like? Was it a wooded area, or what did the scenery look like where you grew up?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Well, at first, you know, it was a wooded area that I remember, and when we were kids, you know, I told you, that white guy that helped us all the time - there were a lot of houses around that area. He had chickens when we were little kids. We would steal the eggs that the chicken laid. [laughs]. We would boil them and eat them. [laughs]. We would do just about anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, me and my friends, when we were growing up, someone had some plants and it was watermelon. We would go get them and that one time we got caught, boy, we took and jumped over the fence. And that one, he was carrying a watermelon. We were running and he was the very last one. And he fell down, [laughs], and the watermelon busted into pieces. We stole that watermelon for no reason. But I guess that's what happens when you steal something.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: One time, we were in Bunch, you know where that's at. We used to steal over there, and we’d pull over somewhere. We would bust them into pieces. It was always in Stilwell, they were laying everywhere. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout where you grew up, were there people living around there close?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: No, not really, but they had some beans everywhere in the field, and he had some Mexicans come over there to pick them. And they would stay there for a very long time. Everyone would all be close by every one of them. Yeah, we all used to do crazy stuff a long time ago. Nowadays, we would all be in jail. [laughs]. All the stuff we did.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, sometimes you think about where you grew up a long time ago?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I used to tell the boys where I used to live, ‘bout a mile where I used to live. I grew up not far from there. Back then, it used to be a wooded area. But now it's all bulldozed out.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout that white guy you said that had that store? Is that where you go sometimes when you're thinkin' bout things?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, that's what I told the kids, that where we live now is a field, and it's right by a church by Cherrytree, and the house is not too far from there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it's really changed a lot now.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, back then they had an Orchard. They called it Stilwell Orchard, and when I was a little boy, I would work there for a little bit. I was probably 12. I would work there sometimes, where they packaged stuff. They taught me how to package stuff like prunes, or peaches - all that stuff. When people find out I knew how to do that stuff, they would hire me. Then I would make a little money doing that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout what we was talkin' bout earlier, that when they cooked that food, like your grandma, and your parents we were talkin' ‘bout, what was your favorite meal that they cooked that you liked the most?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Well, poke salad was pretty good. [laughs].

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee! [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: I ate some last night with beans. They gave me a little gas.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where did you get some poke salad?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Right there, right side of the road.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Back where I come from, man, you can't find any nowhere. They got it all cleared up everywhere where poke salad grew.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, the one I got, it was pretty good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you put eggs in them? ummmmm mannnnn, [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: My grandma always cooked poke salad and wild onion, but I'll just eat ‘bout anything myself.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How ‘bout that uhhh… what do they call it? Watercress? Man, gahhhh.

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, and hot grease and salt. [laughs]. Yeah, sometimes my boys would bring me some stuff like that, or deer meat, because I don't hunt. But my [eldest?] passed away, but they always used to bring me stuff like that. They would bring meat most of the time. I pretty much like just ‘bout pretty much anything, and fish, too. I like to fish, though. But whenever they brought me fish, they were already fixed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Gah-lee, they did a good thing for you, huh? [laughs] Man, you were deboning them, huh? [laughs].

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Boy, my wife, boy, she really likes them, and crawdads, too. They would bring me everything. [laughs]. Those crawdads are really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, this will be the last question I'm gonna ask you. These people that are speaking Cherokee, and you as you were growing up speaking Cherokee, does it sound different from the people that are speaking Cherokee now? Is it different to you?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, nowadays, the ones that are learning Cherokee, me and my wife would listen to them on the phone. I told my wife, “Sometimes I can't understand what they are saying, because we sound ours out a little short and different.” I told her, when they say Osiyo and we say (siyo) not (osiyo), and when they sound something out, they sound it out long and make it hard for me to understand. And when they say, “’Til we meet again,” and then I just tell ‘em, “Same to you.” When I'm talkin' to someone I know real good, we just say the same thing but in a shorter way in Cherokee, say “next time.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That you're sayin' (talegwu) what does that mean?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: It means pretty much till we meet again or I'll see you next time. When I was growing up, that's what they would say to me, just a shorter version of till we meet again. That's all I knew how to say. Or sometimes they say second time till we meet again, they say it really fast. That's the only thing I've noticed, that they make it or sound it out with every sound. They say it different from how I would know how to say it. I just sound it out shorter. My wife tries to learn it, but I told her you can learn it if you really want to, but I told her if you ask me, I say it a lot different than how they would be sayin' it. And some people from Dahlonegah, they say they talk different, and the only way I know is the shorter way of saying things. But they learn Cherokee really good, and I think it's good that they are learning the language nowadays. But I always told my wife, “it would be hard for me to teach you, because like you say, I wish my momma would have taught me”, and she grew up in Chicago, but they were originally from Rocky Mountain. And my mom and dad, that's all they would speak is Cherokee, but they still spoke English OK. But when they talk to me, it was always in Cherokee and my grandma as well, and my sister where I grew up at, all I would hear was Cherokee language. When I started going to school, that’s when they started tryin' to talk or learn English. They wanted me to learn English more, but when it was just me and the boys, all we spoke was Cherokee. But like I said, when we talk, we always talked the short way of saying the words.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This is the last question? What do you think about these people learning how to speak Cherokee? In ‘bout 20 years, do you think the language will still be going?

segments.speaker: jimmy-duncan
segments.translation: Yeah, I think it will, like today, them teaching the language I think it's a good thing. And some of them really want to learn the language, they really do. Like, I don't know how to say it, but when I was growing up, they always used to speak English a lot, but when you got around your friends, then you would speak Cherokee to them. Even in high school that's all they know is English. But again, I think it's really good that they are teaching the Cherokee language.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, the ones that are really trying to learn and that try really hard on learning.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well, I'm glad that we got to talk, and I'm glad that we got to know each other. Thank you, and I'm glad you came and talked to us. Maybe we will see each other again somewhere. And we will talk again then.
